items.title: Tilting your phone changes things differently depending on the order
items.claim: Take a book. Rotate 90 degrees about its vertical axis, then 90 degrees about its horizontal axis. Now reset and reverse the order: horizontal first, then vertical. The book ends up in a DIFFERENT orientation. Rotations in 3D do not commute.

options.text: Rotation matrices in 3D are non-commutative — R1 * R2 is not equal to R2 * R1 in general. SO(3) is a non-abelian Lie group, unlike rotations in 2D which DO commute

items.reveal:
Rotations in 2D (the plane): R(theta1) * R(theta2) = R(theta1 + theta2) = R(theta2) * R(theta1). They commute. The group SO(2) is abelian.

Rotations in 3D: not commutative. The group SO(3) is non-abelian. The order in which you apply rotations changes the final orientation.

Experiment: rotate book 90° about vertical (y-axis) — left becomes back. Then rotate 90° about (now front-pointing) x-axis — back becomes bottom. Reset. Now rotate 90° about x first — top becomes back. Then 90° about y — back becomes left. Final orientations differ.

Mathematically: if R_x is rotation about x-axis and R_y about y-axis, R_x R_y is not equal to R_y R_x. The 'commutator' [R_x, R_y] = R_x R_y - R_y R_x is non-zero, representing a small rotation about the third axis.

Consequences:
- Aerospace: gimbal lock — a 3-axis gyroscope can have its three rotation axes align such that one rotational degree of freedom is lost. Famously almost killed Apollo astronauts on Apollo 11.
- Quaternions (Hamilton 1843) parametrise 3D rotations without gimbal lock and are standard in 3D graphics.
- Quantum mechanics: angular momentum operators have the same commutation structure as 3D rotations, leading to quantisation.

In higher dimensions (n > 3), rotation groups SO(n) are also non-commutative.
items.why: Rotation seems like a simple geometric concept. In 3D it's surprisingly subtle — the order matters, and that fact has cost lives, structured quantum mechanics, and shaped every video game engine.

items.title: In London, there are at least two people with exactly the same number of hairs
items.claim: Humans have at most about 150,000 hairs on their heads. London has over 9 million people. By the pigeonhole principle, at least 60 Londoners share an EXACT hair count.

options.text: If you put more than n items into n containers, at least one container has at least 2 items; more generally, if k*n + 1 items go into n containers, some container has at least k + 1

items.reveal:
The pigeonhole principle (Dirichlet's drawer principle, 1834): if you put n + 1 objects into n boxes, at least one box has at least 2 objects.

Applied to London: ~9 million heads, at most ~150,000 possible hair counts. 9 million divided by 150,000 = 60. So at least 60 Londoners share a hair count exactly.

Elegant applications:
- In any group of 367 people, two share a birthday (366 possible birthdays + leap year).
- Among any 6 people, three are mutual friends or three mutual strangers (a Ramsey theory result, R(3,3) = 6).
- Among any 10 distinct integers from 1 to 100, two have a sum or difference divisible by 17.
- In any sequence of n squared + 1 distinct real numbers, there is a monotone subsequence of length n+1 (Erdős-Szekeres).

The principle gives existence proofs without constructing the example. It's surprisingly powerful for such a simple idea.
items.why: The pigeonhole principle looks obvious but yields non-trivial results — existence guarantees from pure counting, often where direct construction is hopeless.

items.title: sin(1 degree) is irrational
items.claim: Sine of 30°, 45°, 60° are simple expressions like 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2. Sine of 1 degree, 7 degrees, or most other 'nice' integer degree values are irrational numbers with no closed elementary form.
items.prompt: Why are most integer-degree sine values irrational?

options.text: Niven's theorem (1956): the only rational values of sin(theta) for rational theta in degrees occur at multiples of 30 (giving sin = 0, plus/minus 1/2, plus/minus 1). Almost all other rational-degree sines are irrational

items.reveal_title: Niven's theorem and the gaps in trigonometric tables
items.reveal:
Ivan Niven (1956) proved: if both theta (in degrees) and sin(theta) are rational, then sin(theta) is 0, ±1/2, or ±1. By similar argument, cos(theta) rational with theta rational forces cos(theta) in {0, ±1/2, ±1, ±sqrt(2)/2... wait — Niven's actual statement covers SINES specifically}.

The consequence: sin(1°), sin(2°), sin(3°), ... are mostly irrational. Specifically, the standard table of integer-degree sines contains only a few rational values: sin(0°) = 0, sin(30°) = 1/2, sin(90°) = 1, and their reflections (150°, 210°, 270°, 330°). Every other entry in the table is irrational.

This is one reason the SPECIAL ANGLES (30°, 45°, 60°) feature so heavily in geometry: they have simple exact values. Most other angles need decimal approximations.

Closed-form expressions: many integer-degree sines do have closed forms in terms of nested radicals — they're algebraic numbers — but the expressions are ugly. For example, sin(15°) = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4. sin(18°) = (sqrt(5) - 1)/4 (related to the regular pentagon).

For sin(1°): expressible in radicals (it's algebraic, a root of an integer polynomial) but the expression has dozens of nested terms. Modern algebra has tools to compute it exactly; it's just not a useful form.

Why 30° and 45° are special: regular hexagons (60° angles) and squares (45°) tile the plane with simple geometric constructions; the corresponding sine/cosine values come out as simple radicals.

Gauss and constructibility: a regular n-gon is constructible with compass and straightedge if and only if n is a product of powers of 2 and distinct Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537). This is why the 17-gon is constructible (Gauss's first major result, age 19) but the 7-gon and 9-gon aren't.
items.why: Trigonometric tables look like they could be filled with simple values. Almost all entries are deeply irrational, expressible only in nested radicals or numerical approximations. The 'special angles' of school maths are a tiny privileged set.
